跟着留学生リン在便利店打工两年：从打电话约面试到辞职告别，学接客敬语，也读懂严格: Follow international student Lin through two years of working part-time at a convenience store, from calling to set up an interview to quitting and saying goodbye. Learn the keigo used with customers, and come to understand the kindness behind a strict store manager.
打电话约面试: Calling to set up an interview
リン在车站前便利店门口看到「アルバイト募集」的告示，回到宿舍后，把要说的话写在纸: Outside the convenience store in front of the station, Lin saw an 「アルバイト募集」 (part-time help wanted) sign. Back at her dorm, she wrote down what she wanted to say on a sheet of paper, worked up her courage, and made the call. It's three in the afternoon, the store isn't very busy, and the person who picks up happens to be the store manager, Sato. This is her first formal phone call in Japanese since coming to Japan.
便利店「サンライズ」站前店店长，五十多岁，说话直、要求严，但很照顾人: Manager of the station-front branch of the 「サンライズ」 (Sunrise) convenience store; in his fifties, blunt and demanding, but looks out for people
中国留学生，在日本语学校读书，第一次找打工: International student from China studying at a Japanese language school; looking for a part-time job for the first time
这时两人还是「店」和「应聘者」，完全是陌生人。リン要用丁宁语加自谦语（申します、: At this point the two are still just "the store" and "an applicant": complete strangers. Lin needs to use polite language plus humble language (申します, いたします) to lower herself. The manager speaks politely to the applicant but doesn't need to be very formal; he uses ordinary です・ます with a bit of casual speech mixed in now and then, which makes him sound friendly.
感谢您的来电。这里是 Sunrise 站前店，我姓佐藤。: Thank you for calling. Sunrise, Station Front branch. This is Sato speaking.
日本的店接电话，第一句几乎都是「お電話ありがとうございます」＋店名＋自己的名字。: When a Japanese store answers the phone, the first line is almost always 「お電話ありがとうございます」 + the store's name + the person's own name. Hearing this means they're ready, and now it's your turn to say who you are.
百忙之中打扰了。我看到招兼职的告示打来电话，我叫林。: Sorry to bother you when you're busy. I saw that you're looking for part-time staff, and I'm calling about it. My name is Lin.
「お忙しいところすみません」是打给店里、公司时的万能开场。接着马上说清「为什么打: 「お忙しいところすみません」 is the all-purpose opener when calling a store or a company. Follow it right away by making clear "why you're calling" and "who you are." The manager won't have to guess, and will think you're well organized. Jumping straight to "Are you still hiring?" without giving your name comes across as a little abrupt.
啊，是兼职的事吧。谢谢你打来。: Ah, about the part-time job. Thank you for calling.
请问负责招聘的人在吗？: Is the person in charge of hiring available?
不知道对方是谁时，用「ご担当の方」最稳妥。「いらっしゃいますか」是「いますか」的: When you don't know who you're talking to, 「ご担当の方」 is the safest choice. 「いらっしゃいますか」 is the honorific form of 「いますか」, and it's what you use to ask whether someone is there. 「担当の人はいますか」 means the same thing, but it sounds too casual when calling a store.
我就是店长佐藤。现在还在招人哦。: I'm Sato, the manager. We're still hiring, yes.
失礼了。请多多关照。: Oh, excuse me. It's a pleasure to speak with you.
发现对方就是店长，说一句「失礼しました」就够了，不用慌。它的意思是「刚才没认出您: Once you realize the person is the manager, a simple 「失礼しました」 is enough; no need to panic. It means "I didn't realize it was you just now." It's polite and natural, and then you can get straight down to business.
你是学生吗？一周大概能来几次？: Are you a student? About how many times a week can you work?
打工圈里「入る」就是「上班、排进班里」。「入れますか」是它的可能形，问的是「你能: In the part-time job world, 「入る」 means "to work, to be on the schedule." 「入れますか」 is its potential form, and it's asking "how many shifts can you work," not "are you able to enter."
是的，我是日语学校的学生。一周三次，傍晚以后可以上班。: Yes, I'm a student at a Japanese language school. I can work three times a week, from late afternoon on.
那你能先来面试一次吗？明天下午四点怎么样？: Then could you come in for an interview? How about four o'clock tomorrow afternoon?
好的，没问题。是明天下午四点吧。: Yes, that's fine. Four o'clock tomorrow afternoon, right?
时间、地点一定要复述一遍。日本人非常重视「確認」，你复述一次，店长就放心你不会记: Always repeat the time and place back. Japanese people place great importance on 「確認」 (confirming). Repeat it once, and the manager can rest assured you won't get it wrong; if you did get it wrong and show up late, your first impression would be ruined.
请带上简历。照片也要贴好哦。: Please bring your résumé. And put a photo on it, okay?
明白了。简历和照片对吧。: Certainly. A résumé and a photo, right?
「かしこまりました」比「わかりました」更郑重，对店长、客人都能用。第一次通话用它: 「かしこまりました」 is more formal than 「わかりました」 and can be used with both the manager and customers. Using it on your first call shows you're taking things seriously. Later, once you get to know the manager, 「はい、わかりました」 is perfectly fine too.
那么，明天请多关照。我先挂了。: Well then, I look forward to seeing you tomorrow. Goodbye.
日本人打电话以「失礼いたします」结尾。说完别马上挂，数两秒，等对方先挂再轻轻放下: In Japan, phone calls end with 「失礼いたします」. Don't hang up right after saying it: count to two, wait for the other person to hang up first, and then gently put the phone down. Hanging up suddenly with a "click" comes across as cold.
好，等你来。: All right, we'll be expecting you.
店门口的「アルバイト募集」最常见；「まだ募集していますか」= 还在招人吗: 「アルバイト募集」 (part-time help wanted) at a store entrance is the most common use; 「まだ募集していますか」 = Are you still hiring?
「面接を受ける」参加面试，「面接に来る」来面试: 「面接を受ける」 to have an interview; 「面接に来る」 to come for an interview
打工面试几乎一定要带；便利店、百元店就能买到空白格式，照片贴右上角: You almost always have to bring one to a part-time job interview. Blank forms are sold at convenience stores and 100-yen shops; the photo goes in the top right corner
「ご担当の方」= 负责的人，不知道对方名字时这样问: 「ご担当の方」 = the person in charge; ask this way when you don't know the person's name
店里的人直接叫「店長」，不加「さん」也很自然: People who work at the store just call the manager 「店長」; it's natural even without 「さん」
「アルバイトの件で」= 关于兼职的事，打电话、发邮件说明来意时很好用: 「アルバイトの件で」 = about the part-time job; very handy for stating why you're calling or emailing
（打工）上班: to work (a shift at a part-time job)
「シフトに入る」排班上班；「何曜日に入れますか」问哪天能上班: 「シフトに入る」 to work a shift; 「何曜日に入れますか」 asks which days you can work
大约下午四点到天黑；排班常分「早朝」「日勤」「夕方」「夜勤」: Roughly from 4 p.m. until dark; shifts are often divided into 「早朝」 (early morning), 「日勤」 (day), 「夕方」 (evening), and 「夜勤」 (night)
「週三回」一周三次，「週末」周末: 「週三回」 three times a week; 「週末」 weekend
对客人、上级的「わかりました」；对同期说就太硬了: The 「わかりました」 you use with customers and superiors; with coworkers who started at the same time as you, it's too stiff
店里、公司对要来的人说；听到它，说明对方欢迎你来: Said by a store or company to someone who's coming; hearing it means they're glad to have you come
「申す」把自己放低。第一次打电话或面试，对方完全不认识你，用它自我介绍，等于告诉: 「申す」 lowers yourself. On a first phone call or at an interview, when the other person doesn't know you at all, introducing yourself with it tells them "I know my place." With classmates and coworkers who started with you, 「リンです」 is fine; 「申します」 would actually put distance between you.
我是日语学校的小王。: My name is Wang, from the Japanese language school.
信息来源 + を見て + お電話しました: Source of information + を見て + お電話しました
一句话交代清楚「从哪里知道的、为什么打来」。日本人接电话最怕不知道对方来意，你先: In one sentence, it makes clear "where you heard about it and why you're calling." What people answering the phone in Japan dread most is not knowing why the caller is calling. If you say it up front, they can switch right to the right topic, which saves everyone's time and also shows that you're organized.
我是看了招聘网站打来的。: I saw your listing on a job site, so I'm calling.
我看到店里贴的告示打来的。: I saw the notice posted at your store, so I'm calling.
把时间、地点、要带的东西复述一遍，句尾用「ですね」轻轻确认。这不是多余的话，而是: Repeat back the time, the place, and what to bring, ending with 「ですね」 to gently confirm. It isn't unnecessary talk; it tells the other person "I've got it." In Japan, confirming once heads off a lot of misunderstandings and makes people more comfortable leaving things in your hands.
给店铺、公司打电话应聘或咨询时。先说「お忙しいところすみません」，再说来意和名字: When calling a store or company to apply for a job or ask about something. Start with 「お忙しいところすみません」, then give your purpose and your name, repeat the time back once it's set, and finish with 「失礼いたします」.
一接通就问「バイトまだある？」这种朋友口气；不报名字就开始提问。还有人在午饭、傍: Asking 「バイトまだある？」 in a buddy-buddy tone the moment the call connects; starting to ask questions without giving your name. Some people also call during a store's busiest times, like lunch or early evening. Those are best avoided; two or three in the afternoon works better.
店长一天要接很多电话，一听开头就能判断这个人靠不靠谱。来意清楚、会复述确认的人，: A store manager takes many calls a day and can tell from the opening line whether a person is reliable. When someone states their purpose clearly and repeats details back to confirm them, the manager thinks, "This person should be easy to train," and they've earned points before the interview has even started.
在日本，面试其实从打电话那一刻就开始了。店长听的不是你日语多流利，而是你有没有替: In Japan, the interview actually begins the moment you make the phone call. What the manager is listening for isn't how fluent your Japanese is, but whether you're thinking about the other person: avoiding busy times, giving your name first, stating your purpose clearly, repeating the time back. Each one is a small thing, but each tells the other person "I won't cause you trouble." Before calling, Lin wrote her lines out on paper, and by the time she hung up, her palms were soaked with sweat. There's no shame in being nervous; the real pity would be not calling because you're afraid. It's fine to speak a little slowly or make a few mistakes. What the manager values more is the courage it took to pick up the phone.
电话接通，对方说「お電話ありがとうございます、サンライズ駅前店です」。你第一句最: The call connects and the other person says 「お電話ありがとうございます、サンライズ駅前店です」. What's the most appropriate thing to say first?
先说打扰了，再说来意和名字，是最完整的开场。第二个是朋友口气；第三个「いますか」: Apologizing for the bother, then giving your purpose and your name, is the most complete opening. The second sounds like you're talking to a friend; in the third, 「いますか」 isn't respectful enough for a store; the fourth is too abrupt, since they don't even know who you are yet.
店长说「明日の午後四時はどうですか」，你能去。最好的回答是？: The manager says 「明日の午後四時はどうですか」, and you can make it. What's the best reply?
答应之后复述时间，确认无误。只说「はい」也不算错，但少了确认；「かもしれません」: Accept, then repeat the time back to make sure it's right. Just saying 「はい」 isn't exactly wrong, but it skips the confirmation; 「かもしれません」 is vague, and the manager can't plan around it.
不知道负责招聘的是谁，该怎么问？: You don't know who's in charge of hiring. How should you ask?
「ご担当の方」＋「いらっしゃいますか」既尊敬又自然。「責任者を出してください」听: 「ご担当の方」 + 「いらっしゃいますか」 is both respectful and natural. 「責任者を出してください」 sounds like you're about to make a complaint.
